title: Condition of restored Acropora palmata fragments off Mona Island, Puerto Rico, 2 years after the Fortuna Reefer ship grounding
abstract: This study assessed the condition of A. palmata fragments that were reattached following the Fortuna Reefer ship grounding at Mona Island, Puerto Rico. Fragments were monitored for survival and growth over a 2-year period to evaluate the effectiveness of early coral restoration techniques.
key_findings: Two years post-restoration, reattached fragments showed variable survival rates depending on attachment method and location. Fragments secured with epoxy showed better survival than those attached with wire or cable ties. Storm damage and predation by Coralliophila snails were major sources of mortality.

title: New seeding approach reduces costs and time to outplant sexually propagated corals for reef restoration
authors: Chamberland, V.F., Vermeij, M.J.A., Brittsan, M., Carl, M., Schick, M., Petersen, D.
abstract: This study developed a novel approach for rearing sexually produced coral larvae and outplanting settlers of Caribbean coral species. The research focused on reducing the costs and time required to produce corals for restoration through sexual propagation.
key_findings: Sexual propagation of A. palmata is feasible using kreisels and specialized settlement substrates. Outplanting of recently settled individuals showed promising survival when site conditions were suitable. This approach could contribute to restoring genetic diversity in depleted populations when combined with other management tools.

title: Evaluating methods for transplanting endangered elkhorn corals in the Virgin Islands
authors: Forrester, G.E., O'Connell-Rodwell, C., et al.
abstract: This study tested several techniques for transplanting and restabilizing naturally produced A. palmata fragments. Fragments were moved from remnant populations to nearby restoration sites and monitored for survival and growth.
key_findings: Attaching fragments to the reef is beneficial - control fragments left loose died faster and grew slower. Four attachment methods (cable ties, two epoxy types, cement) performed similarly. Clearing surrounding algae improved fragment growth. After 4 years, transplanted fragments grew to ~1,450 cm² and were potentially sexually active. Methods are simple enough for volunteer divers to use.

title: Comparing the efficacy of techniques for transplanting endangered elkhorn coral Acropora palmata
authors: Forrester, G.E., Maynard, A., Schofield, S., Taylor, K.
abstract: This multi-year study compared transplanting techniques across seven years (2005-2011) of coral restoration in the US Virgin Islands. The research examined how survival and growth varied with initial fragment size and time since transplanting.
key_findings: Survival in the first 12 months varied considerably among years. Mortality was highest immediately after transplanting, then declined over time. Initial colony size had a statistically significant but weak effect on survival (explaining only 6% of variance in 12-month growth). Surviving fragments showed progressive size increases over time despite substantial variation.

title: Acropora palmata restoration in the U.S. Virgin Islands: Attachment methods and coral survival
journal: Proceedings of the 11th International Coral Reef Symposium
abstract: This 5-year study compared survival of control and transplanted A. palmata colonies in the US Virgin Islands, examining the effects of attachment methods, site, depth, and colony size on survival outcomes.
key_findings: A. palmata was the only viable candidate for reef rehabilitation among three species tested. Probability of survival increased with colony size. Median survival was 1.3 years for transplants vs 4.3 years for natural colonies (not controlling for size). Site and depth did not significantly affect survival, but colony size and transplant status did. Storm swells were the primary cause of mortality.

title: Improving restoration predictions in complex demographic systems: A population modeling approach
authors: Kuffner, I.B., Lidz, B.H., Hudson, J.H., Anderson, J.S.
abstract: This assisted migration experiment relocated 50 coral fragments of 5 nursery-raised genotypes from the upper Florida Keys to 5 sites across 350 km of the offshore reef, including remote Dry Tortugas sites.
key_findings: All 24 corals relocated to Dry Tortugas survived and calcified ~85% faster than corals at upper Keys sites. While survival did not depend on genotype, there was a weak but significant genetic effect on calcification rate. The native Dry Tortugas genotype was among the fastest growing but not the fastest, suggesting lack of local adaptation at this scale. Dry Tortugas may be a prime location for reestablishing A. palmata.

title: Coral survival after transplantation to a fragmented reef system
authors: Maurer, A.S., Lirman, D., Patterson, J.T.
abstract: This 3-year study monitored coral survival in low-maintenance line nurseries in The Bahamas, assessing both A. cervicornis and A. palmata survival as well as evaluating nursery design durability and cost-effectiveness.
key_findings: Survivorship ranged from 70-97% with significant variation between locations. Initial build-out cost was $22.97 per coral. The nursery design proved durable, withstanding multiple hurricanes with little damage and showing a life expectancy of 5+ years. The design can be maintained with only two site visits per year.

title: Growth and survival of Acropora palmata in nursery and outplanting
authors: Mendoza-Quiroz, S., Padilla-Gamino, J.L., Banaszak, A.T.
abstract: This long-term study (2011-2022) tracked sexually produced A. palmata from larval culture through ex-situ nursery, in-situ nursery, and outplanting onto Mexican Caribbean reefs, monitoring growth, survival, and reproductive maturity.
key_findings: Sexual recruits can be successfully reared and outplanted. By 2019, 53% of colonies were gravid. Outplanted colonies spawned synchronously with wild populations. First documented production of viable F2 offspring from sexually propagated A. palmata. Self-sustaining breeding populations are achievable within approximately 10 years.

title: Monitoring and evaluation of restored Acropora palmata in the Florida Keys
abstract: This thesis studied the dynamics of hurricane-generated A. palmata fragments at three reefs in Puerto Rico over 3 years, examining fragment density, size structure, substrate effects, and mortality rates.
key_findings: Fragment abundance after one year was 369 fragments (1.02 ± 0.35/m²). Mean mortality within the first year was 28.24 ± 3.68%, increasing to 47.96 ± 17.71% after 3 years. Fragment mortality varied significantly between sites (23% at one site vs ~60% at two others). Fragment size differed significantly among reefs but density did not.

title: Survival of Acropora palmata: Balancing growth against mortality
authors: Papke, E., Wallace, B., Walton, C.J.
abstract: This study examined factors affecting growth rates of A. palmata microfragments, specifically comparing plug substrate types (cement vs ceramic) and genetic variation among genotypes.
key_findings: All corals survived and grew, increasing 545% from starting size on average. Corals on cement plugs grew 112% faster than those on ceramic plugs. Significant genetic variation in growth rates was observed, with the fastest genotype growing at 216% the rate of the slowest. Growth was right-skewed with high variation among individuals.

title: Artificial substrates to minimize handling stress during coral transplantation
authors: Pausch, R.E., Williams, D.E., Miller, M.W.
abstract: Two experiments examined effects of A. palmata outplant characteristics and habitat on restoration success, coinciding with thermal stress events in 2014 and 2015 that provided insight into environmental interactions with coral restoration.
key_findings: Smaller fragments produced more live tissue area, experienced less bleaching, and had equal survivorship compared to larger fragments. Genotypes varied significantly in survivorship, bleaching severity, and growth. One genotype (CN2g) performed well across all metrics; another (SLg) performed poorly. Fore reef habitat showed less severe bleaching than patch reef. Fragments did not consistently perform better at their site of origin.

title: Demographic rates of Acropora palmata in restoration
authors: Rosales, S.M., Williams, D.E., Miller, M.W.
abstract: This study examined four A. palmata genotypes at three Florida Keys restoration sites, correlating environmental factors (nutrients, currents, temperature, chlorophyll) and coral microbiome composition with outplant survivorship.
key_findings: Environmental factors correlated with survivorship: shallow depth and increased current velocity were associated with higher survival. The relative abundance of Rhodobacterales bacteria in coral tissues was inversely proportional to outplant survivorship. Results inform site selection decisions to increase restoration success.

title: Effects of genotype and environment on Acropora palmata dynamics
authors: Roth, L., Muller, E.M., van Woesik, R.
abstract: This study compared fragmentation dynamics and population responses of A. palmata in the US Virgin Islands with corymbose Acropora in Aka Jima, Japan, examining how thermal stress events affect size-frequency distributions.
key_findings: A. palmata showed much higher fragmentation rates than Indo-Pacific corymbose Acropora. The 2005 thermal stress event shifted size distributions toward smaller colonies through increased fragmentation. By 5 years later, distributions shifted back toward larger colonies as survivors grew. A. palmata tends to fragment and survive during thermal stress, while Indo-Pacific Acropora undergo mortality without fragmentation.

title: Monitoring coral restoration: Performance metrics and best practices
authors: Schutter, M., Croquer, A., Villamizar, E.
abstract: This study tested specific pre-outplanting aquaculture regimes (feeding with Artemia, bicarbonate addition) to determine their effects on post-outplanting survival and growth of A. palmata sexual recruits.
key_findings: The most successful treatment (9 weeks aquaculture with feeding) doubled both survivorship and recruit size compared to ambient conditions (20% vs 10% survival; 8 vs 4 polyps per recruit). Larger recruit size resulted in higher post-outplanting survival due to increased resistance to biofouling. Ambient aquaculture still exceeded natural conditions where no natural recruitment was observed.

title: The impacts of Coralliophila abbreviata on Acropora palmata dynamics
abstract: This dissertation examined the population dynamics of A. palmata in the Florida Keys from 2004-2010, creating population matrix models and simulating hurricane impacts and outplanting scenarios.
key_findings: Percent cover, colony number, and dominance by large individuals all declined throughout the study period. Elasticity analysis showed that largest individuals have greatest contribution to population growth rate. Population depletion is predicted if severe hurricanes return every 20 years or less. Outplanting can provide positive population trajectory short-term, especially if colonies are reared several years before transplanting.

title: Coralliophila abbreviata predation on elkhorn coral and restoration implications
authors: Vardi, T., Williams, D.E., Sandin, S.A.
abstract: This study conducted annual demographic surveys of A. palmata in the northern Florida Keys from 2004-2010, creating population matrix models that included a severe hurricane year (2005-2006) and simulating various outplanting scenarios.
key_findings: Population metrics (cover, colony number, large-colony dominance) all declined through the study. Matrix models predict population depletion given hurricane return times of 20 years or less. Elasticity analysis confirms large individuals have the greatest influence on population growth rate. Active outplanting can achieve positive population trajectory short-term, particularly with pre-reared colonies.

title: Stabilization of fragments and substrates for coral restoration
abstract: This study tested whether stabilizing naturally occurring A. palmata fragments could increase their performance (tissue survival and growth) compared to unstabilized controls.
key_findings: Stabilized fragments lost significantly less tissue and ranked higher in overall performance than unstabilized controls. Epoxy and cable ties were similarly effective for stabilization. Epoxy can be safely applied in contact with live tissue and is rapidly overgrown. Cable ties require suitable substrate with attachment points. Stabilization preserves live tissue and enhances fragment growth.
